headline: Holgate's south cut reformed overnight — fluke steady, bass gone nocturnal
subhead: A fresh cut off the Holgate refuge line is reshaping the drift, while daytime heat pushes stripers into the dark and fluke keep grinding on the sod banks.
body_markdown:
I walked the south end at Holgate Tuesday morning on the low and the beach told me something changed. There's a new cut about 200 yards north of the last refuge marker, cutting through what used to be a solid bar. Last week's onshore blow and the building tides into the full moon reshaped that whole stretch — we said the tides would sharpen things up going into the full moon, and here's the proof, a fresh trough scoured out with a hard rip line running off the point on the outgoing. That kind of structure change is exactly what you want to find before everyone else does. I marked it on the phone, walked it at low again this morning to see how it held, and it's still there. Depth in the trough is running four to six feet over sand, dropping to eight where it meets the channel edge. That's a bass spot after dark and a fluke spot on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up onto the flat.

Speaking of fluke — that bite hasn't skipped a beat. Bucktail and fluke-belly combos are still doing work in the Barnegat Inlet rips, same pattern we flagged last week, and it's translated well into Little Egg too. I've been running a half-ounce white bucktail with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet in white or pink shad behind it, dragged slow along the channel edges off Graveling Point in 12 to 18 feet on the last of the outgoing. Keepers are mixing with shorts pretty consistently — not a blitz, but steady enough that a couple hours on the drift usually puts two or three fish over 18 inches in the cooler. The sod banks in Great Bay proper, particularly around the mouth of the Mullica where it dumps into the bay, are holding fish too on live killies fished on a simple three-way rig, 10 to 12 feet of water, moving with the tide instead of anchoring dead still.

Striped bass have gone underground, literally and behaviorally. Surface temps in the low-to-mid 70s across the back bay and inlet have shoved them off the daytime program — I'm not seeing much worth chasing in the surf between sunup and sundown right now. The better play has been bunker chunks fished after dark around the rocks at Barnegat Light and along the bridge structure at the Causeway, where current breaks up against the pilings and creates a cooler seam even in August heat. Guys working that pattern from 9 PM to 1 AM on the outgoing have been finding slot fish, occasionally something bigger, holding tight to structure where the current slows just enough for an ambush. That new cut at Holgate I mentioned — I'd bet money it starts holding bass on the outgoing once the water cools a touch more overnight, especially once we get past this full moon push and into slightly calmer nights.

Bluefish are the one species that doesn't care about the heat, and they've been the most reliable daytime action on the beat. Choppers mixed with smaller cocktail blues are working the inlet rips at Barnegat Light and along the surf line from Ship Bottom down to Beach Haven, especially on the first two hours of the incoming when bait gets funneled through the inlet mouth. Metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything in the one to two ounce range — worked fast through the wash has been drawing strikes, and if you want to save your leaders, wire or heavy fluoro is not optional right now. There's a real wave of blues pushing down the coast and it's showing here the same way it's showing everywhere else on the Jersey side.

Weakfish have been thin but not absent — a few legal fish coming out of the deeper holes in Great Bay on live mullet and killies, mostly incidental catches while fluke fishing rather than a targeted bite worth planning a trip around. Kingfish are still showing in the surf wash at Ship Bottom and Beach Haven on bloodworms and Fishbites, small but consistent, a good option if you've got kids on the beach and want steady rod-bending action without much fuss.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a major shift over the next several days unless we get a wind shift or a cold front that breaks up this warm surface layer. The fluke bite should hold on the sod banks and inlet structure as long as the water stays stable, and I'd keep working that new Holgate cut on the outgoing tide to see how it develops — cuts like that either fill back in within a couple weeks or become a real feature for the rest of the season. Building tides toward the new moon will add current strength, which should sharpen both the inlet fluke bite and give the bluefish more current to work with in the rips. For bass, night trips with bunker chunks around structure remain the higher-odds play until something cools this water down. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be at that new cut two hours before dark with a bucktail in hand, watching to see if the bass find it before the fluke crowd does.
